interactions.mechanism: St. John's wort induces P-gp and CYP3A pathways that can lower direct oral anticoagulant exposure. Lower exposure can reduce protection against stroke or venous thromboembolism.
interactions.management: Avoid St. John's wort with apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban unless the prescriber explicitly manages the interaction. Do not start or stop St. John's wort without notifying the anticoagulant prescriber.
interactions.evidence_notes: DailyMed labeling for apixaban and rivaroxaban explicitly names St. John's wort among combined P-gp/CYP3A inducers to avoid; dabigatran and edoxaban labels warn against P-gp inducers that reduce exposure.

interactions.mechanism: Potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes add to the potassium-retaining effect of potassium-sparing diuretics, increasing risk of severe hyperkalemia and arrhythmia.
interactions.management: Avoid potassium supplements and potassium salt substitutes with spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone, amiloride, or triamterene unless specifically prescribed with serum potassium monitoring.
interactions.evidence_notes: Spironolactone labeling warns against potassium supplementation and high-potassium salt substitutes because of hyperkalemia risk.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's wort can induce P-glycoprotein activity and reduce digoxin exposure. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic range, so reduced concentrations can compromise heart failure or atrial fibrillation control.
interactions.management: Avoid adding St. John's wort to digoxin therapy without prescriber oversight. If unavoidable, monitor serum digoxin concentration and clinical response when St. John's wort is started or stopped.
interactions.evidence_notes: Human pharmacokinetic evidence and digoxin labeling support a clinically relevant reduction in digoxin concentration with St. John's wort.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium can chelate tetracycline-class antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk.
interactions.management: Separate calcium supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.management: Separate iron supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.management: Separate magnesium supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Zinc can chelate tetracycline-class antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk.
interactions.management: Separate zinc supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Green tea catechins, especially EGCG, can inhibit intestinal uptake transporters and markedly reduce nadolol exposure. Human studies report reduced nadolol plasma exposure and reduced blood-pressure effect.
interactions.management: Avoid concentrated green tea extract with nadolol. For brewed green tea, consult the prescriber about timing and blood pressure monitoring rather than assuming separation fully prevents the interaction.
interactions.evidence_notes: Human pharmacokinetic studies show substantial nadolol exposure reduction with green tea or EGCG-concentrated green tea extract.

interactions.mechanism: Iron can chelate fluoroquinolone antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk during an active infection.
interactions.management: Separate iron supplements from ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and related fluoroquinolones by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.
interactions.evidence_notes: Current ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin DailyMed labels instruct separation from iron-containing products because absorption is reduced.

interactions.mechanism: Magnesium can chelate fluoroquinolone antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk during an active infection.
interactions.management: Separate magnesium supplements or magnesium-containing antacids from ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and related fluoroquinolones by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.
interactions.evidence_notes: Current ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin DailyMed labels instruct separation from magnesium-containing products because absorption is reduced.

interactions.mechanism: Vitamin K is required to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Warfarin reduces vitamin K activity. A sudden increase in vitamin K intake can reduce the anticoagulant effect; a sudden decrease can increase it.
interactions.management: This is a consistency warning, not a ban. Keep vitamin K intake from food and supplements about the same each day. Tell your prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting, stopping, or changing any supplement containing vitamin K; INR monitoring may be needed after a change. Do not change warfarin on your own.
interactions.evidence_notes: Vitamin K directly antagonizes warfarin mechanism. This is stated on every warfarin drug label. NIH ODS Vitamin K fact sheet explicitly warns anticoagulant users.

interactions.mechanism: Fish oil can have antiplatelet effects at high doses and might affect INR with warfarin. NIH ODS notes that most research at 3–6 g/day does not significantly affect anticoagulant status and reviews have not found clinically significant bleeding overall. A case report describes bleeding after a fall with 6 g/day omega-3 plus aspirin and warfarin; it does not establish a warning threshold.
interactions.management: Tell your prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting, stopping, or changing fish oil while taking warfarin. Periodic INR monitoring may be appropriate, and watch for unusual bruising or bleeding. Do not change warfarin on your own. This alert identifies the combination; it does not mean a proven dose threshold was crossed.
interactions.evidence_notes: PMID 17192169 is a case report with aspirin, warfarin and high-dose omega-3 after a fall. Neither that report nor NIH ODS establishes a 1 g/day warning floor or a universal 3 g/day bleeding threshold.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgo may increase bleeding risk with warfarin. A large Veterans Administration record study found an association with bleeding during concurrent use, while the literature has mixed and conflicting findings. Observational association does not establish causality, incidence for an individual or a safe dose.
interactions.management: Avoid adding ginkgo during warfarin treatment without anticoagulation-clinician review. If already taking it, discuss monitoring and changes rather than adjusting warfarin yourself. Report unusual bruising or bleeding promptly.

verification.notes: 26958257 directly studies ginkgo with warfarin; 40198642 did not include a warfarin cohort and is removed as direct support for this pair. Observational evidence and conflicting literature remain qualified.

interactions.evidence_notes: Mixed: observational data suggest increased bleeding risk, but controlled studies at recommended doses show no significant effect. Severity reflects precautionary approach for anticoagulant users.

interactions.mechanism: Garlic supplements may affect platelet function and increase bleeding risk with warfarin. The cited monographs do not establish a 600 mg safe-below threshold or clinically demonstrated CYP2C9 inhibition.
interactions.management: Talk to your warfarin prescriber before starting, stopping or changing garlic supplements. Ask whether INR checks are needed and report unusual bruising or bleeding.
interactions.evidence_notes: Mainly case reports. Culinary amounts are safe. Concentrated supplements may have mild antiplatelet effect.

interactions.mechanism: St. John’s wort can induce drug-metabolizing pathways and reduce warfarin exposure or anticoagulant effect. Starting or stopping it can therefore change anticoagulation; the reviewed evidence does not establish one exclusive enzyme/transporter mechanism for all warfarin responses.
interactions.management: Avoid adding St. John’s wort during warfarin treatment without the anticoagulation clinician reviewing it. If already taking it, tell the clinician before any change so INR monitoring can be planned. Do not change warfarin or discontinue an established supplement without discussing the monitoring plan.

interactions.mechanism: Vitamin E can inhibit platelet aggregation and antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. NIH notes that large supplemental doses may increase bleeding risk with warfarin, but the amount needed for a clinically significant effect is uncertain.
interactions.management: Contains vitamin E. Large supplemental doses may increase bleeding risk with warfarin, but the amount that causes a clinically significant effect is uncertain. Tell your prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting, stopping, or changing this supplement, and keep your use consistent — extra monitoring may be appropriate after a change. Do not change warfarin on your own. This alert reflects the presence of vitamin E; it does not mean a known dose limit was crossed.

interactions.mechanism: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K2 and may exert a mild pro-coagulant effect, potentially reducing warfarin's efficacy. Case reports describe decreased INR when CoQ10 is added to warfarin therapy.
interactions.management: Monitor INR if starting CoQ10 while on warfarin. Dose adjustments may be needed. Inform your prescriber.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor and uncertain INR signal; retain as background context without gating product fit.
interactions.mechanism: Case reports suggest glucosamine (alone or with chondroitin) may increase INR in warfarin users. The mechanism is not well established; possible mild CYP2C9 inhibition or direct effect on coagulation cascade.
interactions.management: Monitor INR when starting glucosamine. Report any unusual bruising or bleeding. Effect may be small but warrants awareness.

interactions.mechanism: Cranberry juice and extracts may inhibit CYP2C9, the primary enzyme responsible for warfarin (S-enantiomer) metabolism. This can elevate warfarin levels and INR. Case reports include fatal hemorrhage.
interactions.management: Limit cranberry consumption to small amounts (occasional serving of juice/food). Avoid large quantities of cranberry juice or concentrated supplements. Monitor INR closely if intake changes.

interactions.mechanism: Curcumin has antiplatelet effects in laboratory and animal studies. This provides a precautionary basis for possible bleeding effects with warfarin, but does not establish a human oral 500 mg interaction threshold.
interactions.management: Inform your warfarin prescriber before starting, stopping or changing turmeric or curcumin supplements. Ask about INR monitoring and report unusual bruising or bleeding.

interactions.mechanism: One case report described more than a twofold rise in INR/prothrombin time after dong quai was added to stable warfarin, with improvement after discontinuation. The authors state that the true mechanism remains unknown; a single report cannot establish incidence or a safe dose.
interactions.management: Avoid adding dong quai during warfarin treatment without anticoagulation-clinician review. Tell the clinician if already taking it so INR monitoring and any changes can be managed. Do not adjust warfarin yourself; report unusual bruising or bleeding promptly.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor dose-dependent bleeding signal; culinary and lower supplemental exposure should not gate product fit.
interactions.mechanism: Human platelet studies of ginger have mixed results. A possible bleeding interaction with warfarin warrants caution, but a 2 g/day safe-below boundary is not established.
interactions.management: Discuss ginger supplements with your warfarin prescriber. Report unusual bruising or bleeding and ask whether INR monitoring is appropriate when changing supplement use.
interactions.evidence_notes: Theoretical based on in-vitro platelet inhibition. Clinical evidence for interaction at dietary doses is weak.

interactions.mechanism: St. John’s wort induces drug-metabolizing enzymes and can reduce the effect of CYP3A4-metabolized statins. Human evidence reports reduced simvastatin exposure and increased LDL cholesterol during atorvastatin co-use. Lovastatin shares CYP3A4 metabolism, a mechanistic scope inference; these findings do not apply uniformly to every statin.
interactions.management: Avoid adding St. John’s wort to atorvastatin, simvastatin or lovastatin without prescriber review. The clinician should manage treatment and any lipid monitoring; do not change the statin yourself. This rule does not establish the same interaction for pravastatin or rosuvastatin.

verification.notes: Atorvastatin study measured lipid response, not drug concentrations. Review 15260917 distinguishes reduced simvastatin exposure from unchanged pravastatin pharmacokinetics. Lovastatin is a metabolism-based inference. Exact IN identities verified live; no broad statin-class exclusion.

interactions.evidence_notes: PMID 17701167 measures lipid outcomes, not plasma atorvastatin pharmacokinetics. No universal 50% class-wide exposure reduction is established by that study.

interactions.mechanism: Red yeast rice may contain monacolin K, which is chemically identical to lovastatin. The amount varies substantially across products and may be undisclosed. Combining a monacolin-containing product with a prescription statin can add statin exposure and increase muscle, liver and kidney adverse-effect risks; it does not predictably double the statin dose.
interactions.management: Do not use red yeast rice if you are already taking a prescription statin. If you prefer a natural approach, discuss with your doctor — the two should not be combined. Seek immediate care for severe muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine.

verification.notes: Wave 6.Y Batch 9.A. PMIDs content-verified via PubMed efetch 2026-05-27. 36779111 is a direct case report of RYR-induced rhabdomyolysis; 40909457 documents severe RYR-induced rhabdomyolysis with AKI + respiratory failure (severity tail justifying Major); 33538260 is the JACC focus seminar on RYR for hypercholesterolemia documenting the monacolin K = lovastatin equivalence the mechanism text relies on. Official NCCIH + FDA sources retained as primary regulatory anchor.

interactions.mechanism: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit irreversibly inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, increasing bioavailability of CYP3A4-metabolized statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin, lovastatin). This raises statin plasma levels and muscle toxicity risk.
interactions.management: Simvastatin labeling says to avoid grapefruit juice. Lovastatin labeling warns that grapefruit juice raises lovastatin levels and myopathy risk. Atorvastatin labeling advises against large quantities (more than 1.2 liters a day). Pravastatin, rosuvastatin, and fluvastatin are not significantly affected. Spacing simvastatin or lovastatin from grapefruit juice can reduce but does not remove the effect. Spacing atorvastatin does not reliably reduce the effect. Dose spacing is not a substitute for the label precautions above.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice can raise blood levels of some statins by slowing an enzyme in the gut that breaks them down. The effect is large with simvastatin and lovastatin; with atorvastatin it matters mainly with large amounts of juice (more than 1.2 liters a day). Higher statin levels can raise the chance of muscle aches or weakness.
interactions.practical_guidance: On simvastatin, skip grapefruit juice. On lovastatin, ask your prescriber before having grapefruit. On atorvastatin, avoid large amounts (more than 1.2 liters a day). Pravastatin, rosuvastatin and fluvastatin aren't affected by grapefruit.

interactions.mechanism: Statin labeling reports myopathy and rhabdomyolysis with lipid-modifying nicotinic acid doses of at least 1 g/day. Trials of high-dose niacin added to statin therapy also provide adverse-event evidence; they do not establish a universal safe lower dose.
interactions.management: Use lipid-modifying nicotinic acid with a statin only under prescriber supervision. Report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine promptly. This regulatory dose qualifier does not establish the same interaction for niacinamide, other B3 forms, or universal safety at lower doses.

dose_threshold.rationale: Rosuvastatin labeling reports myopathy/rhabdomyolysis with lipid-modifying niacin doses of at least 1 g/day. This label threshold does not establish universal safety below it.

interactions.evidence_notes: Approved form/context extension October13. The lipid-modifying nicotinic-acid label qualifier is evaluated only from complete canonical form and dose facts; explicit niacinamide is excluded from this pair-specific claim. Mixed or unknown forms retain review; no estimate of the nicotinic-acid fraction is invented. Other B3 profile risks remain independent.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort has serotonergic activity. Combining it with an SSRI or SNRI can cause serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening. Symptoms can include agitation, high temperature, muscle rigidity or clonus, and seizures.
interactions.management: Do not combine St. John's Wort with an SSRI or SNRI without specialist direction. Any change or switch must be planned by your prescriber; the required washout depends on the medicines and clinical circumstances. Do not stop your prescribed antidepressant on your own. Seek emergency care immediately if serotonin syndrome symptoms appear.

interactions.mechanism: 5-HTP is a serotonin precursor, and MSK advises against unsupervised use with serotonergic medicines including SSRIs. A reported sertraline case involved multiple medicines/supplements and exercise; it supports a serious concern but not a pair-specific incidence or numerical safe dose.
interactions.management: Do not add 5-HTP during SSRI treatment without prescriber review. Do not stop or switch antidepressants yourself; any washout depends on the exact medicine. Suspected serotonin syndrome, including agitation with fever, muscle rigidity or altered consciousness, requires emergency care.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: SAMe may interact with serotonin-increasing medicines, including SSRIs. This supports a potential serotonin-syndrome precaution; the retained content does not establish a quantified human combination risk or the asserted case-report incidence.
interactions.management: Avoid combining SAMe with SSRIs without medical supervision. If used as an adjunct (some practitioners do this), requires careful dose titration and monitoring for agitation, tremor, or hyperthermia.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgo may affect hemostasis, and bleeding is a concern with SSRIs, but the cited hospital study did not establish a specific SSRI-ginkgo effect or a 120 mg interaction boundary. This pair remains a mechanistic precaution, not proven serotonin toxicity.
interactions.management: Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to review ginkgo with the exact SSRI and other bleeding risks. Do not change the SSRI yourself or assume a lower ginkgo dose establishes no interaction. Report unusual bruising or bleeding.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.background_rationale: Drug-specific sedation monitoring signal; keep visible as background context without a categorical product verdict.
interactions.mechanism: Fluvoxamine strongly inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme metabolizing melatonin. Fluvoxamine with melatonin can substantially increase melatonin exposure and cause excessive sedation.
interactions.management: Ask the fluvoxamine prescriber before using melatonin. If the combination is approved, use only the dose they recommend and monitor for excessive drowsiness; do not drive or operate machinery if impaired.
interactions.evidence_notes: In a small healthy-volunteer study, oral melatonin 5 mg with fluvoxamine 50 mg increased melatonin AUC about 17-fold and peak concentration about 12-fold. This is a drug-specific exposure study; it does not establish a class-wide SSRI effect or a safe melatonin dose.

interactions.mechanism: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion, causing potassium retention. Additional potassium supplementation can lead to dangerous hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium), causing cardiac arrhythmias and potentially cardiac arrest.
interactions.management: Do not take potassium supplements while on ACE inhibitors without medical supervision. Avoid potassium-based salt substitutes. Regular serum potassium monitoring is essential if any potassium supplementation is used.

interactions.mechanism: Glycyrrhizin-containing licorice can increase blood pressure and reduce potassium, potentially undermining blood-pressure treatment. A systematic review/meta-analysis found these effects with chronic glycyrrhizic-acid ingestion; NCCIH warns that people with hypertension can have serious effects even with small amounts.
interactions.management: Avoid glycyrrhizin-containing licorice during blood-pressure treatment unless the clinician has reviewed it. A product described as deglycyrrhizinated (DGL) is a different preparation, but the label must establish that identity; do not assume an unspecified licorice product or DGL is universally safe.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Ephedrine-alkaloid supplements have been associated with serious cardiovascular and central-nervous-system adverse events, including hypertension and stroke. FDA prohibits these dietary supplements because of unreasonable risk. The cited adverse-event review does not establish a beta-blocker-specific unopposed-alpha mechanism.
interactions.management: Do not use dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids. Ask a clinician to review the product and medicines if already using one; chest pain, severe headache or neurological symptoms require emergency care.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.evidence_notes: General ephedrine-alkaloid hazard is sourced; beta-blocker-specific mechanism and risk magnitude are not established by the cited study.

interactions.mechanism: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, increasing plasma levels of CYP3A4-metabolized calcium channel blockers (felodipine, nifedipine, amlodipine). Elevated CCB levels can cause excessive blood pressure lowering, dizziness, and reflex tachycardia.
interactions.management: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice with CYP3A4-metabolized calcium channel blockers. Effects can last 24–72 hours after consuming grapefruit. Check with your pharmacist about your specific CCB.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Grapefruit slows down how your body processes some blood pressure medicines (felodipine, nifedipine, amlodipine), so more of the drug ends up in your bloodstream. This can cause dizziness, flushing, or low blood pressure.
interactions.practical_guidance: Skip grapefruit and grapefruit juice while on these medicines. The effect can last 1–3 days, so timing the dose around grapefruit doesn't really help.

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence modest blood-pressure effect; informational monitoring only.
interactions.mechanism: A Cochrane review of two small trials found no clinically significant blood-pressure reduction with CoQ10. A clinically useful additive effect with antihypertensive medicines and a 100 mg interaction threshold are not established.
interactions.management: Tell your prescriber if you use CoQ10 with blood-pressure medicines. Monitor your blood pressure when changing supplements; medication changes should be made by your prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Alpha-lipoic acid may affect glucose control. A trial across 300–1200 mg/day does not establish a 600 mg safe-below interaction boundary with metformin or other diabetes medicines.
interactions.management: Discuss alpha-lipoic acid with your diabetes prescriber and monitor glucose when starting or changing it. Adjust prescribed medicine only under prescriber supervision.

interactions.mechanism: Chromium might lower blood glucose. With insulin or other diabetes medications, the additive effect could increase the risk of low blood glucose.
interactions.management: Chromium might lower blood glucose, which may add to diabetes medication effects. Ask the diabetes clinician whether additional glucose monitoring is appropriate when starting or changing supplemental chromium. Do not change medicines yourself; studied dose ranges do not establish a 200 mcg/day interaction boundary.

verification.notes: September26 accepted LEDGER D8 requires an effect-specific clinical boundary. The older disclosed screening gate has no later exception and its source does not establish a clinical cutoff; removed under existing policy. No lower-dose safety guarantee.

interactions.background_rationale: Potential additive glucose lowering supports monitoring, not a categorical product-level caution.

interactions.mechanism: A small pilot study found glucose-lowering effects of berberine in type 2 diabetes, including use alongside existing treatment. Additional glucose lowering is a concern with diabetes medicines, but this study does not establish a class-wide rate or dose boundary for hypoglycemia.
interactions.management: Have the diabetes clinician review berberine before combining it with treatment and agree on appropriate glucose monitoring. Report symptoms of low blood sugar and follow the existing treatment plan. Do not reduce or replace diabetes medicines yourself.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Glucose effects of bitter melon vary by preparation. A small trial of a specific mcIRBP-19 fruit extract reported borderline overall glucose results and a positive subgroup; it does not establish a universal 600 mg interaction threshold.
interactions.management: Discuss bitter melon with your diabetes prescriber and monitor glucose when starting or changing the supplement. Do not replace prescribed therapy; medication changes require prescriber supervision.

interactions.mechanism: A meta-analysis of heterogeneous fenugreek seed trials suggests possible glucose lowering, with limitations in study quality and preparation reporting. Additive effects with diabetes medicines are a precaution; a generic 500 mg safe-below boundary is not established.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose when using fenugreek seed supplements with diabetes medicines. Inform your prescriber, who should manage any medication adjustment.

interactions.mechanism: A small study using 400 mg/day of a particular Gymnema leaf extract alongside diabetes therapy reported reduced glucose and medication requirements. It did not compare doses that establish an interaction boundary, and the result cannot be generalized to every preparation.
interactions.management: Have the diabetes clinician review Gymnema and plan glucose monitoring before use with treatment. Do not reduce or replace diabetes medicines yourself or assume less than 400 mg/day guarantees no interaction.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.background_rationale: Uncertain glucose interaction signal retained as background context; no validated safe-below dose is established.
interactions.mechanism: Trials of cinnamon preparations report variable glucose effects. The preferred preparation and dose remain unclear; an additive glucose-lowering effect with diabetes medicines is a precaution, not a proven dose boundary.
interactions.management: Discuss supplemental cinnamon with your diabetes prescriber and monitor glucose. Do not use it instead of prescribed treatment. Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which can be harmful with substantial exposure.
interactions.evidence_notes: PMID 14633804 has an expression of concern (PMID 40834253), not a retraction. PMID 24019277 reports heterogeneous doses and uncertain preferred dose; neither establishes a 500 mg interaction threshold.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium forms insoluble complexes with levothyroxine in the GI tract, reducing its absorption by about 20–25% when taken together. This can result in inadequately controlled hypothyroidism.
interactions.management: Take levothyroxine at least 4 hours before or after calcium supplements. Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast. Monitor thyroid function tests if supplementation regimen changes.

interactions.mechanism: Ferrous sulfate and other iron supplements form insoluble complexes with levothyroxine in the GI tract, reducing levothyroxine absorption significantly. This is a well-documented interaction affecting thyroid control.
interactions.management: Take levothyroxine at least 4 hours before or after iron supplements. Monitor TSH levels after starting or stopping iron. Women often take both and need to manage this timing carefully.

interactions.mechanism: Magnesium can bind levothyroxine in the GI tract and reduce its absorption. In a 2025 crossover trial, magnesium aspartate lowered levothyroxine absorption by 12% and magnesium citrate by 7% (not significant), a smaller effect than reported for calcium or iron.
interactions.management: Take magnesium supplements at least 4 hours away from levothyroxine. Morning levothyroxine with evening magnesium is a practical approach.

interactions.mechanism: Soy isoflavones and soy protein can impair levothyroxine absorption and may also affect thyroid hormone metabolism. The effect is most pronounced in infants but relevant at high supplemental doses in adults.
interactions.management: Separate levothyroxine from soy-rich foods or supplements by at least 4 hours. Patients with hypothyroidism on stable levothyroxine should have TSH re-checked if starting high-dose soy isoflavone supplements.

verification.notes: PMID 16571087 (Messina & Redmond, Thyroid 2006) content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27 — title matches the soy-thyroid interaction claim. Replaces prior empty source_pmids that violated critical_no_hallucinated_citations.

interactions.mechanism: Coffee, particularly espresso, can reduce levothyroxine absorption when taken simultaneously. Polyphenols and other coffee compounds may interfere with GI absorption.
interactions.management: Take levothyroxine with water only, at least 30–60 minutes before coffee. This is a standard clinical recommendation for all thyroid patients.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Coffee, especially espresso, can reduce how much levothyroxine your body absorbs when you take them close together. This isn't dangerous, but it can mean your thyroid medicine doesn't work as well.
interactions.practical_guidance: Take levothyroxine with water on an empty stomach, and wait at least 30–60 minutes before having coffee or breakfast.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's wort induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and can reduce exposure to susceptible transplant immunosuppressants. Cyclosporine-associated transplant rejection has been reported. The retained sources do not establish an identical 50–70% reduction for every listed drug.
interactions.management: Do not use St. John's wort with transplant immunosuppressants. Contact the transplant prescriber promptly after accidental use; they should arrange the appropriate immunosuppressant drug-level monitoring and treatment review. Do not stop or adjust prescribed treatment yourself.

interactions.mechanism: Echinacea may interact with immunosuppressants through effects on immune activity. NCCIH describes this interaction as theoretical; the cited content does not establish transplant rejection or autoimmune flare caused by this combination.
interactions.management: Avoid echinacea with any immunosuppressant therapy. Transplant patients and those on immunosuppressants for autoimmune conditions should not use echinacea for colds or immune support.

interactions.mechanism: Cat's claw (Uncaria tomentosa) has immunostimulant properties that may oppose immunosuppressive therapy, potentially reducing drug efficacy in transplant or autoimmune patients.
interactions.management: Avoid cat's claw with immunosuppressants. Inform prescriber of all herbal supplements being taken.

interactions.mechanism: Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus) has documented immunomodulatory effects, including upregulation of T-cell and NK cell activity. This may counteract immunosuppressive drugs in transplant or autoimmune patients.
interactions.management: Avoid astragalus with immunosuppressant therapy. Discuss all herbal supplements with your transplant or rheumatology team.

interactions.mechanism: Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, increasing blood levels of cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and sirolimus. Elevated immunosuppressant levels increase toxicity risk (nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, infection risk).
interactions.management: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice with transplant immunosuppressants. Maintain consistent dietary patterns; avoid sudden changes in grapefruit intake.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Grapefruit raises the level of transplant medicines (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus) in your blood. Even small changes in level matter for these drugs because they have a narrow safe range.
interactions.practical_guidance: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice entirely while on transplant immunosuppressants. Be consistent — even occasional grapefruit can shift your levels.

interactions.mechanism: Long-term phenytoin therapy can lower folate status. Folate supplementation can lower serum phenytoin concentrations in some people, potentially affecting seizure control.
interactions.management: If you take phenytoin, discuss folate intake and any supplement dose with the prescribing clinician. Do not start high-dose folic acid on your own; phenytoin levels or seizure control may need monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgotoxin (4'-O-methylpyridoxine) in ginkgo seeds and some leaf preparations can lower seizure threshold. Additionally, ginkgo may induce CYP2C19, potentially reducing valproate levels.
interactions.management: Use ginkgo with caution in patients with seizure history. Seizure monitoring is recommended. High-quality, standardized ginkgo leaf extract with controlled ginkgotoxin levels is preferable.

interactions.mechanism: Tyramine-rich food can provoke a hypertensive crisis with MAOIs that impair dietary tyramine metabolism. Dietary restrictions depend on the exact medicine, route and dose; they are not identical for all MAOIs.
interactions.management: Confirm the exact MAOI, route and dose with the prescriber and follow its food instructions. EMSAM 6 mg/24 hours does not require a modified diet only when 9 or 12 mg/24 hours has not been used during the previous 2 weeks; EMSAM 9 or 12 mg/24 hours requires avoidance of tyramine-rich foods, continuing for 2 weeks after stopping or reducing to 6 mg/24 hours. Other MAOIs have different instructions. This food exception is not clearance for concentrated tyramine supplements. Severe headache, chest pain or neurological symptoms require emergency care.

interactions.management: Do not add St. John’s wort during MAOI treatment without prescriber review. Switching or stopping treatment requires an exact-medicine plan; there is no universal supplement-to-MAOI washout established by these sources. Suspected serotonin syndrome requires emergency care.

MSK reports mania with an MAOI and 5-HTP and serotonin syndrome with linezolid, an antibiotic MAOI; these reports do not establish a class-wide event rate or safe dose.
interactions.management: Do not add 5-HTP while using an MAOI without the prescriber reviewing it. Do not stop or switch the MAOI yourself; any product-specific washout must follow the exact medicine and a clinician-directed plan. Suspected serotonin syndrome requires emergency care.

interactions.management: Do not combine SAMe with an MAOI. Do not stop or change a prescribed MAOI to use SAMe; the prescriber must manage any medication change or product-specific washout.

interactions.management: Have the prescriber review ginseng before combining it with an MAOI. The evidence is limited and does not establish a safe dose or a universal washout period. Do not change prescribed MAOI treatment yourself.

interactions.management: Discuss garlic supplements with your prescriber if you use NSAIDs regularly. Watch for unusual bruising or gastrointestinal bleeding.

interactions.mechanism: A retrospective hospital study reported bleeding-related associations involving ginkgo and selected NSAIDs. It does not establish causality for every NSAID or an interaction-onset boundary at 120 mg/day of ginkgo.
interactions.management: Have a clinician or pharmacist review ginkgo with the exact NSAID and other bleeding risks. Report unusual bruising or bleeding. Do not assume a dose below 120 mg/day removes the concern.

interactions.mechanism: Willow bark contains salicin-derived constituents. EMA advises against concomitant salicylates or other NSAIDs without medical advice. Willow bark is not chemically equivalent to aspirin, and the monograph does not establish an exact doubled dose or numerical interaction boundary.
interactions.management: Avoid adding willow bark to an NSAID without medical review. Ask the clinician or pharmacist to review the preparation and other medicines. Black stools, vomiting blood or other significant bleeding require urgent medical care.

interactions.mechanism: Valerian may have sleep-inducing effects and should not be combined with alcohol or sedatives without clinician guidance. NCCIH does not establish an oral 400 mg interaction threshold.
interactions.management: Avoid valerian with prescription sedatives or sleep medications. Do not drive or operate machinery if using both. Inform your doctor.

interactions.mechanism: Kava has sedative effects. NCCIH advises against combining it with other sedative substances, including benzodiazepines and alcohol. A published report concerns coma with alprazolam and kava, but does not quantify risk across every sedative. Kava-associated liver injury is a separate concern, not proof that all sedatives amplify it.
interactions.management: Avoid combining kava with sedative medicines or alcohol without prescriber review. Do not drive if impaired or abruptly stop a prescribed sedative. Severe drowsiness, difficulty breathing or inability to wake needs emergency care.

interactions.mechanism: Passionflower can cause drowsiness and may add to nervous-system slowing from sedating medicines or anesthesia. NCCIH does not establish a 400 mg interaction threshold.
interactions.management: Avoid passionflower with sedative medications. Do not drive after combining. Use under physician guidance.

interactions.mechanism: Glycyrrhizin inhibits 11-beta-HSD2, which normally inactivates cortisol in peripheral tissues. Combined with corticosteroids, this increases the effective glucocorticoid activity and exacerbates potassium loss, fluid retention, and hypertension.
interactions.management: Avoid licorice root supplements with corticosteroid therapy. Monitor blood pressure and potassium. DGL licorice has reduced glycyrrhizin and is safer.

interactions.mechanism: Echinacea stimulates immune function including cytokine production. Corticosteroids are used to suppress immune responses. These opposing mechanisms may reduce therapeutic efficacy of corticosteroids.
interactions.management: Avoid echinacea with corticosteroid therapy for immune suppression (transplant, autoimmune). For short-course corticosteroids (allergies, asthma exacerbation), the interaction is less critical but still worth noting.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, accelerating the metabolism of estrogen and progestin components of oral contraceptives. This reduces OC plasma levels and may cause contraceptive failure, leading to unintended pregnancy.
interactions.management: Do not use St. John's Wort with oral contraceptives. Use a backup contraceptive method if concurrent use occurred. Discuss with your prescriber regarding timing before resuming reliance on OC alone.

interactions.mechanism: Chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus) acts on dopamine receptors to reduce prolactin and may modulate progesterone and LH secretion. This hormonal activity may interfere with oral contraceptives' progestin-mediated effects.
interactions.management: Avoid chasteberry with hormonal contraceptives. The interaction is theoretical but relevant given chasteberry's hormonal activity. Inform your OB/GYN.

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence high-dose isoflavone signal; dietary soy should not produce an alert.
interactions.mechanism: Genistein is a soy isoflavone with estrogen-receptor activity. A clinically important interaction with oral contraceptives and a 100 mg interaction threshold are not established by the retained source.
interactions.management: Discuss concentrated genistein supplements with your prescriber if you use oral contraceptives. The retained evidence does not establish contraceptive failure or a safe-below supplement dose.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium competitively inhibits iron absorption in the small intestine by competing for DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1) and potentially forming insoluble complexes. Both heme and non-heme iron absorption are reduced when taken simultaneously with calcium.
interactions.management: Take iron and calcium supplements at different times — at least 2 hours apart. Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach in the morning. Calcium can be taken with meals or at bedtime.

interactions.mechanism: Tea polyphenols can reduce non-heme iron absorption when consumed with an iron-containing meal. A small study in iron-replete women found about 37% inhibition with concurrent brewed tea; this is not a 50–90% effect established for all green-tea extracts and iron supplements.
interactions.management: Avoid taking iron with tea. Follow the iron product directions and ask your clinician about timing. A one-hour tea interval attenuated inhibition in a meal study; it did not establish a universal interval for concentrated green-tea extracts.
interactions.evidence_notes: PMID 29046302 studied brewed tea with porridge in 12 nonanemic iron-replete women, not a concentrated green-tea extract/iron-supplement combination.

interactions.mechanism: High supplemental zinc intake over time can reduce copper absorption and status. ODS describes this effect with zinc doses of 50 mg or more over weeks; the adult zinc upper limit is not a proven copper-deficiency onset boundary.
interactions.management: Long-term higher-dose zinc can reduce copper status. Ask a clinician whether your dose and duration warrant copper monitoring or a balanced formulation. The sources do not establish a 25 mg safe-below boundary; this review does not mean that every low-dose zinc/copper combination causes harm.

interactions.mechanism: St. John’s wort and 5-HTP both affect serotonin. MSK advises avoiding their combined use to reduce the risk of excessive serotonin. The fluoxetine/triptan/hypericum report is not evidence for this two-supplement pair, and the pair-specific incidence is unknown.
interactions.management: Avoid combining St. John’s wort with 5-HTP without clinician review. Do not use this warning as advice to choose either supplement as treatment. Suspected serotonin syndrome, including agitation with fever, muscle rigidity or altered consciousness, requires emergency care.

interactions.mechanism: 5-HTP increases serotonin synthesis as a direct precursor. SAMe is involved in monoamine neurotransmitter metabolism and may interact with supplements that increase serotonin. Combining them can add serotonergic load and increase serotonin-syndrome risk.
interactions.management: Avoid combining 5-HTP with SAMe unless a clinician is deliberately supervising serotonergic supplement use. Watch for agitation, tremor, diarrhea, fever, sweating, or confusion if they were taken together.
interactions.evidence_notes: MSK and NCCIH describe serotonin-risk concerns for 5-HTP/SAMe and advise avoiding multiple serotonin-affecting supplements; direct pair evidence is limited, so this remains a precautionary Major stack warning.

interactions.mechanism: Rat hepatic-cell and mouse experiments found that certain kava extracts potentiated acetaminophen toxicity. In the mouse experiment flavokawains A and B reproduced the effect, whereas the tested kavalactone dihydromethysticin did not. These preclinical findings do not establish the magnitude or dose boundary of the combination risk in humans or the same effect for every purified kavalactone.
interactions.management: Ask a clinician or pharmacist to review kava with acetaminophen, especially with repeated use or liver risk. Risk may depend on the preparation; labels often do not establish flavokawain content. Do not assume a low dose or a kavalactone percentage establishes absence of risk. Symptoms of possible liver injury need prompt medical assessment.

The Epidiolex label does not establish a warfarin-specific warning; its tested CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 substrates did not show clinically significant exposure changes.

interactions.management: Inform your prescriber of CBD use and monitor blood pressure when starting or stopping it. Any medication adjustment should be managed by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: A clinically demonstrated increase in statin exposure from CBD is not established by the retained source. The Epidiolex label does not anticipate OATP1B1/1B3 inhibition, and its tested CYP3A4 substrate had unchanged exposure. Statin-specific clinical evidence remains limited.
interactions.management: Tell your statin prescriber about CBD use. Report new muscle pain or weakness; any medication change should be made by your prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Vinpocetine inhibited P-glycoprotein in vitro; the clinical relevance is uncertain. CYP inhibition occurred above expected human exposures, making a clinical CYP interaction unlikely (PMID 28930203). A small study in 18 healthy men found only a minute warfarin effect, considered unlikely to have clinical implications (PMID 2272713). These findings do not establish clinically important potentiation across the anticoagulant class; this warning is precautionary.
interactions.management: Avoid starting vinpocetine while taking warfarin or another anticoagulant unless your prescriber is managing the combination. If you already take both, tell your anticoagulation clinician and ask whether additional monitoring is needed.

interactions.mechanism: St. John’s wort can reduce exposure to some HIV medicines through enzyme/transporter induction. In healthy volunteers, one indinavir study found mean AUC and trough reductions of 57% and 81%. Those values are specific to indinavir and that preparation; they are not measurements for every protease inhibitor. Reduced exposure could compromise treatment.
interactions.management: Avoid adding St. John’s wort during HIV treatment without review by the HIV prescriber or pharmacist. They must check the exact regimen and manage any change. Do not stop antiretroviral treatment yourself.

interactions.mechanism: In severely immunocompromised patients, live probiotic bacteria (particularly Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) carry a risk of bacteremia or sepsis (rare but reported). The risk is greatest with Saccharomyces boulardii (fungemia risk) in immunocompromised hosts.
interactions.management: Avoid probiotics containing live organisms in severely immunocompromised patients (transplant, chemotherapy). Discuss with transplant or oncology team. Heat-killed probiotics or postbiotics are safer alternatives.

interactions.mechanism: Panax ginseng may reduce the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. A controlled trial found ginseng reduced warfarin AUC and INR. The mechanism may involve CYP induction or direct procoagulant ginsenoside effects.
interactions.management: Monitor INR closely if taking ginseng with warfarin. INR may need to be checked more frequently and warfarin dose adjusted.

interactions.mechanism: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion. Combined with vitamin D, they can increase hypercalcemia risk, particularly with kidney impairment, hyperparathyroidism or older age. The adult vitamin D upper limit is not an interaction-onset threshold.
interactions.management: Ask the prescriber to review vitamin D supplementation with a thiazide diuretic and determine whether calcium or kidney-function monitoring is appropriate. Do not assume an amount below 4000 IU/day removes this interaction concern.

interactions.mechanism: Magnesium-containing products can interfere with absorption of oral bisphosphonates. This gastrointestinal interaction does not establish a warning for intravenous bisphosphonates; dosing instructions differ by oral medicine and formulation.
interactions.management: Follow the exact oral bisphosphonate label and ask the pharmacist to schedule magnesium. Immediate-release products have their own fasting and separation instructions. Risedronate delayed-release is taken after breakfast, and magnesium supplements or laxatives must be taken at a different time of day. Do not apply a universal fasting interval to every formulation.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgo constituents can affect platelet function. A retrospective observational study found associations between ginkgo drug interactions and bleeding, including aspirin and clopidogrel combinations. These associations do not establish causation or a quantified risk for every patient.
interactions.management: Avoid combining ginkgo with antiplatelet drugs unless your prescriber specifically recommends it. Tell your surgical team about ginkgo before any procedure and follow their instructions on when to stop it. Do not stop a prescribed antiplatelet on your own.
interactions.evidence_notes: PMID 40198642 is a retrospective observational study, not a systematic review. The avoid tier is precautionary; the study does not establish a universal preoperative stop interval.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium ions can form poorly absorbed complexes with oral ciprofloxacin, reducing ciprofloxacin exposure and risking antibiotic treatment failure.
interactions.management: Take oral ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium-containing supplements, multivitamins, or antacids, as directed by the prescription label.

interactions.mechanism: Zinc can bind oral fluoroquinolones in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing antibiotic absorption and risking treatment failure.
interactions.management: Separate oral fluoroquinolones from zinc-containing supplements and multivitamins. The timing interval differs by drug, so follow the prescription label or pharmacist instructions; do not apply one interval to the entire class.

interactions.mechanism: Combining an MAOI with an SSRI can cause life-threatening serotonin syndrome. MAOIs differ in selectivity, reversibility and route, but the reviewed antidepressant labels contraindicate the combination.
interactions.management: Do not combine an MAOI with an SSRI. A prescriber must plan switching using the exact medicine labels. Fluoxetine labeling requires at least 14 days after stopping an antidepressant MAOI before starting fluoxetine and at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI; other medicines have their own intervals. Do not stop or switch treatment yourself. Suspected serotonin syndrome requires emergency care.

interactions.mechanism: Meperidine labeling contraindicates use with MAO inhibitors or within 14 days after stopping them because severe, sometimes fatal reactions can occur, including serotonin toxicity.
interactions.management: Do not combine meperidine with an MAOI or use it within 14 days after stopping an MAOI. The prescriber must select an appropriate analgesic after reviewing all medicines; another opioid is not automatically a safe replacement. Seek emergency care for suspected serotonin toxicity or severe breathing impairment.

interactions.mechanism: Amphetamine and methylphenidate labeling contraindicates use with MAO inhibitors because hypertensive crisis can occur. Exact instructions depend on both medicine labels; this is not evidence that every MAOI has an identical interaction profile.
interactions.management: Do not combine these medicines without urgent prescriber review. The reviewed stimulant labels prohibit use during MAOI treatment and for 14 days after stopping an MAOI. Switching in the other direction must follow the exact labels and a clinician-directed plan. Severe headache, chest pain or neurological symptoms require emergency care.

interactions.mechanism: Trimethoprim has antifolate effects that raise concern with methotrexate. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole labeling advises avoiding methotrexate co-use; its sulfonamide component can displace methotrexate from protein binding and compete with renal transport. That combination-label evidence does not quantify the risk of trimethoprim alone.
interactions.management: Avoid adding trimethoprim or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole during methotrexate treatment without specialist review. The clinician must choose an antibiotic and any blood-count or kidney-function monitoring; other antibiotics are not automatically safe alternatives. Fever, mouth sores, unusual bruising or severe weakness need urgent medical assessment.

interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and can increase ergotamine exposure. Ergotamine labeling contraindicates the combination because of ergot toxicity, vasospasm and ischemia.
interactions.management: Do not combine ergotamine with erythromycin. Contact the prescriber promptly to select treatment appropriate to the infection and migraine history. Severe limb pain, cold or pale extremities, or chest pain require urgent medical evaluation.

interactions.mechanism: NSAIDs can increase bleeding risk during anticoagulant treatment through effects on platelets and gastrointestinal injury. Anticoagulant labels warn about concomitant NSAID use; risk depends on the medicines and patient context.
interactions.management: Avoid adding an NSAID without the anticoagulation prescriber reviewing it. If both are prescribed, the clinician should choose the dose, duration and monitoring. Seek urgent care for major bleeding, black stools or vomiting blood. Do not stop a prescribed anticoagulant on your own.

The clinician should determine any dose change from measured concentrations and clinical response. Do not adjust lithium yourself. New tremor, vomiting, confusion or difficulty walking needs prompt medical assessment.

interactions.mechanism: Diuretic-induced sodium loss can reduce lithium clearance and increase serum lithium concentrations; the lithium label addresses diuretics beyond thiazides. Lithium toxicity can occur near therapeutic concentrations, so a single numerical toxicity boundary is not reliable.
interactions.management: Have the prescribing clinician review this combination and arrange more frequent lithium monitoring; electrolyte and kidney-function checks may also be needed. The clinician should determine any dose change from measured concentrations and clinical response. Do not adjust lithium yourself. New tremor, vomiting, confusion or difficulty walking needs prompt medical assessment.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.evidence_notes: Thiazide diuretics reduce lithium clearance, causing accumulation and toxicity. This interaction is stated on lithium drug labels and is a standard pharmacology teaching point.

interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and can increase simvastatin exposure, with myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk. Erythromycin labeling contraindicates concomitant simvastatin.
interactions.management: Do not combine simvastatin with erythromycin. Contact the prescribing clinician promptly to arrange an appropriate antibiotic or clinician-directed statin interruption. Unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine requires urgent medical assessment.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Ondansetron and levofloxacin labels warn about QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Combined QT effects are a concern, especially with low potassium or magnesium, bradycardia, cardiac disease or other QT-prolonging medicines; individual risk is not quantified by these labels.
interactions.management: Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to review whether both medicines are needed and whether ECG or electrolyte monitoring is appropriate. Do not change prescribed treatment yourself. Fainting or a new irregular heartbeat requires prompt medical assessment.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Spironolactone (potassium-sparing diuretic) blocks aldosterone and reduces urinary potassium excretion. ACE inhibitors also reduce aldosterone levels via the renin-angiotensin system. Combined, both agents retain potassium independently, producing additive hyperkalemia — which can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias.
interactions.management: Use this combination with caution only when clinically indicated (e.g., heart failure post-RALES). Monitor serum potassium and creatinine closely — within 1 week of starting and after any dose change. Avoid potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes.

interactions.mechanism: Triptan labeling warns that serotonin syndrome can occur with SSRIs, but does not contraindicate this pair. A large observational study found a low incidence among patients coprescribed triptans and SSRIs/SNRIs; that does not eliminate the possibility of a serious reaction.
interactions.management: Ask the prescribing clinician to review the combination and explain symptoms to watch for, particularly when treatment starts or doses change. Do not stop prescribed treatment or assume a lower dose removes the risk. Suspected serotonin syndrome, including agitation with fever, muscle rigidity or altered consciousness, requires emergency care.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Iodinated contrast procedures can be associated with acute kidney-function deterioration, allowing metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis. The metformin label requires interruption for specified renal, medical-history or contrast-route risk factors, not every intravenous contrast procedure.
interactions.management: Tell the imaging team and prescribing clinician that you take metformin. The label calls for a hold at or before iodinated contrast when eGFR is between 30 and 60 mL/min/1.73 m², there is a history of liver disease, alcoholism or heart failure, or contrast is intra-arterial. The clinician should reassess kidney function 48 hours after imaging and restart only if stable. Do not decide the hold or restart yourself; unknown renal or procedure details require review.

verification.notes: Corrected to metformin label risk factors. Existing pairwise consumer does not automatically evaluate renal function, contrast route or history; presence warning remains a request for clinician review, not an instruction that all IV contrast requires interruption.

interactions.evidence_notes: Current September 2026 FDA label is the rule authority. IV versus intra-arterial exposure and renal/history context matter. ACR guidance is less restrictive for some IV procedures; this rule does not silently adopt that alternative or infer an actual procedure from metformin use alone.

medication_exceptions.notes: Confirm with the imaging team for this actual procedure: intravenous iodinated contrast, current eGFR above 60, no acute kidney injury, and no history of liver disease, alcoholism or heart failure. If any fact is unknown, leave this unconfirmed. Do not change metformin yourself.

interactions.mechanism: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 activation of clopidogrel and reduces its antiplatelet activity. Clopidogrel labeling advises avoiding omeprazole and esomeprazole; separating doses by 12 hours does not eliminate the documented effect.
interactions.management: Avoid this combination unless the prescribing clinician has reviewed it. Ask the clinician or pharmacist to select an appropriate acid-reducing medicine if needed; do not change clopidogrel or stomach treatment on your own.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Fluconazole can increase exposure to CYP3A4-metabolized statins such as atorvastatin and simvastatin, and to CYP2C9-metabolized fluvastatin, increasing myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk. Lovastatin shares CYP3A4 metabolism, a mechanistic scope inference. This is not a uniform clinically important interaction with every statin.
interactions.management: Have the prescriber or pharmacist review the exact statin, fluconazole course and doses before combining them. Statin-specific labeling may call for dose limits, adjustment or monitoring rather than a universal prohibition. Do not stop or replace a statin on your own. Seek prompt medical advice for unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine.

verification.notes: Fluconazole label names atorvastatin/simvastatin and fluvastatin. Lovastatin inclusion is a CYP3A4-based inference, not a claimed direct pair trial. Rosuvastatin study 12451430 reports small changes not considered clinically relevant; pravastatin and rosuvastatin excluded from this pair. Fluvastatin label permits a limited dose with fluconazole; no blanket stop instruction.

interactions.mechanism: Beta blockers reduce heart rate and AV conduction via beta-1 blockade. Verapamil (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) independently slows SA and AV node conduction. Combined, additive negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects can produce severe bradycardia, heart block, or asystole — particularly with IV administration.
interactions.management: Use together only when clinically necessary with careful monitoring. Avoid IV verapamil in patients on beta blockers. Monitor heart rate and ECG at initiation and dose changes. Dose reductions of one or both agents may be required.

interactions.mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4, reducing renal and non-renal digoxin clearance. Digoxin plasma levels can rise 70–100% within days of starting amiodarone, pushing into the toxic range (>2 ng/mL). Digoxin toxicity causes bradycardia, heart block, and potentially fatal arrhythmias.
interactions.management: Reduce the digoxin dose by 30–50% when starting amiodarone. Monitor digoxin levels closely within 1 week and again after 1 month. Maintain levels in the 0.5–0.9 ng/mL therapeutic range for heart failure.

interactions.mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the primary enzyme responsible for theophylline metabolism. CYP1A2 inhibition can double theophylline plasma levels, causing theophylline toxicity: nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, seizures.
interactions.management: If ciprofloxacin is required in a patient on theophylline, reduce theophylline dose by 30–50% and monitor serum theophylline levels. Use an alternative antibiotic when possible (azithromycin has minimal CYP1A2 inhibition).

interactions.mechanism: In a randomized trial of patients on stable warfarin, repeated acetaminophen at 2 g/day or 3 g/day for 10 days increased INR compared with placebo, with a significant increase by day 3. These studied doses do not establish a safe-below cutoff or prove the same effect for every anticoagulant.
interactions.management: Tell the warfarin prescriber before repeated acetaminophen use, including over-the-counter combination products, so INR monitoring can be arranged if needed. Do not assume 2 g/day or a lower dose guarantees no interaction, and do not adjust warfarin yourself. Report unusual bruising or bleeding promptly.

verification.notes: Primary source content reviewed for the corrected claim. Presence screening is not a declaration of harm at every dose or clinical clearance.

interactions.mechanism: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine, topiramate) upregulate CYP3A4 and conjugation enzymes, markedly accelerating metabolism of ethinyl estradiol and progestins in combined oral contraceptives. The result is reduced OC plasma levels and failure to suppress ovulation — unintended pregnancy.
interactions.management: Counsel patients on the interaction. Consider higher-dose OC formulations, additional barrier contraception, or switch to a non-hormonal or long-acting reversible contraceptive (IUD, implant) that is not affected by enzyme induction.

interactions.mechanism: A complex bidirectional interaction: valproic acid displaces phenytoin from protein binding (raising free phenytoin transiently) and inhibits CYP2C9-mediated phenytoin metabolism (raising total phenytoin). Simultaneously, phenytoin induces valproate metabolism, lowering valproate levels. Net effect is unpredictable changes in both drug levels, risking toxicity or loss of seizure control.
interactions.management: Monitor both free phenytoin and valproate levels when used together. Dose adjustments for both agents are typically required. Neurologist oversight is essential. Avoid initiating both simultaneously — introduce one at a time with careful level monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Corticosteroids impair gastric mucosal defense by reducing prostaglandin synthesis and mucus production. NSAIDs further inhibit COX-1-dependent mucosal protection. Combined, the risk of gastric and duodenal ulcers, GI bleeding, and perforation increases approximately 15-fold compared to either agent alone.
interactions.management: Add a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) when corticosteroids and NSAIDs must be used together. Minimize duration and dose of NSAIDs. Consider switching to acetaminophen for analgesia when anti-inflammatory effect is not required.

interactions.mechanism: Antipsychotics cause CNS and respiratory depression. Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A inhibition, producing sedation and respiratory suppression. Combined, additive CNS depression can cause excessive sedation, respiratory depression, aspiration, and death. clozapine and IV lorazepam have been specifically associated with fatal cardiorespiratory collapse.
interactions.management: Avoid parenteral combination. For oral use, use the lowest necessary doses of both agents, monitor respiratory status, and avoid in patients with sleep apnea or compromised respiratory reserve. Alert patients and caregivers to signs of excessive sedation.

interactions.mechanism: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin stores (by blocking serotonin reuptake transporter SERT on platelets), impairing platelet aggregation. NSAIDs further impair platelet function via COX-1 inhibition and cause GI mucosal erosion. Combined use raises the risk of upper GI bleeding 3–15 fold compared to either drug alone.
interactions.management: Add a PPI when SSRIs and NSAIDs are co-prescribed, particularly in patients over 65 or with prior GI bleeding. Consider acetaminophen as an alternative analgesic for patients on SSRIs.

interactions.mechanism: Alcohol inhibits gluconeogenesis and increases lactate production by shifting NAD+/NADH ratio. Metformin also reduces hepatic lactate clearance. Heavy or binge alcohol intake combined with metformin increases lactic acidosis risk, especially in patients with hepatic impairment, renal insufficiency, or dehydration. Note: this is a lifestyle drug interaction.
interactions.management: Advise patients on metformin to avoid heavy or binge drinking. Moderate alcohol consumption (1–2 standard drinks/occasion) is generally acceptable in the absence of hepatic or renal impairment. Reinforce hydration, especially during illness.

interactions.mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics cause renal potassium and magnesium wasting. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia both increase myocardial sensitivity to digoxin's toxic effects at any given serum level — AV block, ventricular arrhythmias, and even therapeutic levels become toxic when electrolytes are depleted.
interactions.management: Monitor serum potassium and magnesium regularly in patients on digoxin plus loop or thiazide diuretics. Replace electrolytes promptly. Consider potassium-sparing strategies. Target potassium >4.0 mEq/L in digoxin-treated patients.

interactions.mechanism: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1 hepatic uptake transporter, dramatically increasing plasma concentrations of many statins (especially simvastatin, cerivastatin, rosuvastatin). Elevated statin levels substantially increase the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. This combination caused cerivastatin's market withdrawal in 2001.
interactions.management: Avoid gemfibrozil with most statins. If combined lipid-lowering therapy is required, fenofibrate has significantly lower interaction potential. If gemfibrozil is necessary, use pravastatin at the lowest effective dose with vigilant myopathy monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, causing sodium and water retention and vasoconstriction. This blunts the blood pressure-lowering effect of most antihypertensive drug classes (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, diuretics, CCBs). Blood pressure can rise significantly, even with occasional NSAID use.
interactions.management: Avoid chronic NSAID use in patients with hypertension. For analgesic needs, acetaminophen is preferred. If NSAIDs are used short-term, monitor blood pressure closely and counsel patients to track home readings.

interactions.mechanism: Benzodiazepines and opioids both depress the central nervous system. Combined use can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death; FDA warnings apply even to prescribed use.
interactions.management: Avoid combining these medicines unless the prescriber has reviewed the need and arranged careful monitoring. Do not suddenly stop prescribed benzodiazepines or opioids. Methadone or buprenorphine treatment for opioid use disorder should not be withheld solely because a benzodiazepine is used; the treatment team must manage the risk. Ask whether an opioid overdose reversal medicine is appropriate. Trouble breathing or inability to wake requires emergency care.

verification.notes: FDA 2020 communication supports the serious CNS-depression concern and cautions against withholding opioid-use-disorder treatment. Opioid IN membership verified via live RxNorm/RxClass, excluding nonopioid sleep agents, antagonists and nonopioid antitussives. No lower-dose safe boundary established.

interactions.mechanism: Cholestyramine can bind concomitant oral medicines in the gut and delay or reduce the absorption of warfarin. Starting, stopping, or changing the timing of cholestyramine can therefore change warfarin exposure and anticoagulant control.
interactions.management: Take warfarin at least 1 hour before or 4 to 6 hours after cholestyramine unless the anticoagulation clinician gives different instructions. Keep the timing consistent and contact the warfarin prescriber or anticoagulation service when starting, stopping, or changing cholestyramine; INR monitoring may be needed. Do not change warfarin on your own.

verification.notes: RxNorm live properties verified RxCUI 2447 as cholestyramine resin and RxCUI 11289 as warfarin. DailyMed explicitly names warfarin and gives the asymmetric oral-drug timing interval.

interactions.evidence_notes: Current DailyMed cholestyramine labeling states that cholestyramine may delay or reduce warfarin absorption and directs other oral drugs at least one hour before or four to six hours after cholestyramine.
